                                   3    II.        LEGAL STANDARD
                                   4          A.      Motion to Dismiss
                                   5               Under Rule 12(b)(1), a party may move to dismiss a claim based on subject matter

                                   6   jurisdiction, including a lack of standing. Chandler v. State Farm Mut. Auto Ins. Co., 598 F.3d

                                   7   1115, 1121–22 (9th Cir. 2010). “On a motion to dismiss for a lack of standing, a district court

                                   8   must accept as true all material allegations in the complaint, and must construe the complaint in

                                   9   the nonmovant's favor.” Id. (citing Bernhardt v. Cnty. of Los Angeles, 279 F.3d 862, 867 (9th Cir.

                                  10   2002)). The party asserting federal subject matter jurisdiction bears the burden of establishing that

                                  11   it is present. Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co., 511 U.S. 375, 377 (1994).

                                  12               “The constitutional minimum of standing” requires three elements. Lujan v. Defenders of
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555, 560-61 (1992). First, the plaintiff must prove that “an injury-in-fact, i.e., a

                                  14   concrete and particularized, actual or imminent invasion of a legally protected interest.” Id. at 555.

                                  15   Second, there must be a “causal connection” between the injury and the conduct. Id. at 560. The

                                  16   injury must be “traceable to the challenged action of the defendant and not the result of the

                                  17   independent action of some third party not before the court.” Id. (cleaned up). Finally, the plaintiff

                                  18   must show that the injury “will likely be redressed by a favorable decision.” Chandler, 598 F.3d at

                                  19   1122.

                                  20               To establish an injury in fact, the plaintiff must show that both that the injury is

                                  21   particularized and that it is concrete. Lujan, 504 U.S., at 560. For an injury to be particularized, it

                                  22   must “affect the plaintiff in a personal and individual way.” Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330,

                                  23   339 (2016). For the injury to be concrete, it must actually exist. Id. at 340 (internal citations

                                  24   omitted).

                                  25           B.       Plaintiffs’ Privacy Claims
                                  26               Plaintiffs bring both common law and statutory claims based on Capital One’s conduct:

                                  27                   i.   Negligence - Count 1

                                   1          “To state a claim for negligence in California, a plaintiff must establish the following

                                   2   elements: (1) the defendant had a duty, or an ‘obligation to conform to a certain standard of

                                   3   conduct for the protection of others against unreasonable risks,’ (2) the defendant breached that

                                   4   duty, (3) that breach proximately caused the plaintiff’s injuries, and (4) damages.” Bass v.

                                   5   Facebook, Inc., 394 F. Supp. 3d 1024, 1038–39 (N.D. Cal. 2019) (internal citations omitted).

                                   6              ii.     Violation of CCPA - Count 6
                                   7          The CCPA provides a limited civil cause of action for any “consumer whose nonencrypted

                                   8   and nonredacted personal information… is subject to an unauthorized access and exfiltration,

                                   9   theft, or disclosure as a result of the business’s violation of the duty to implement and maintain

                                  10   reasonable security practices.” Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.150(a)(1). Under the CCPA, “[a] third

                                  11   party shall not sell or share personal information about a consumer that has been sold to, or shared

                                  12   with, the third party by a business unless the consumer has received explicit notice and is provided

                                  13   an opportunity to exercise the right to opt-out.” Id. § 1798.115.

                                  14              iii.    Unjust Enrichment - Count 9

                                  16   the defendant received an unjustly retained a benefit at the plaintiff’s expense.” Katz-Lacabe v.

                                  17   Oracle Am., Inc., 668 F. Supp. 3d 928, 945 (N.D. Cal. 2023).

                                   3          The ECPA “prohibits unauthorized ‘interception’ of an ‘electronic communication.’”

                                  12              vi.   Pleading Standard for Privacy Claims
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          Because Plaintiff’s “claims . . . rely on the same underlying injury,” the Court “need not

                                  14   repeat its standing analysis” for each of Plaintiff’s theories of liability. Garmong v. Tahoe Reg’l

                                  15   Plan. Agency, 806 F. App’x 568, 571 (9th Cir. 2020); see also Krzyzek v. OpenX Techs., Inc., No.

                                  16   25-cv-05588, 2026 WL 206855, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 27, 2026) (analyzing Article III standing as

                                  17   a threshold issue on all claims where plaintiffs brought a putative class action for common law

                                  18   privacy claims, unjust enrichment, violations of CIPA, and ECPA).

                                  19          To determine whether Plaintiffs have alleged a concrete privacy injury “courts should

                                  20   assess whether the alleged injury to the plaintiff has a ‘close relationship’ to a harm ‘traditionally’

                                  21   recognized as providing a basis for a lawsuit in American courts.” Popa v. Microsoft Corp., 153

                                  22   F.4th 784, 789 (9th Cir. 2025). Two analogous common-law privacy torts include the torts of

                                  23   intrusion upon seclusion and public disclosure of private facts. To show intrusion upon seclusion,

                                  24   a plaintiff must show “an intentional interference with his interest in solitude or seclusion, either

                                  25   as to his person or as to his private affairs or concerns, of a kind that would be highly offensive to a

                                  26   reasonable man.” Nayab v. Cap. One Bank (USA), N.A., 942 F.3d 480, 491 (9th Cir. 2019)

                                  27   (emphasis added) (quoting Restatement (Second) of Torts § 652B cmt. a (Am. Law Inst. 1977)).

                                  28   Similarly, a claim for public disclosure of private facts requires that a defendant “gives publicity”
                                                                                          6
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05985-TLT            Document 304          Filed 05/22/26      Page 7 of 14




                                   1   to a matter that concerns “the private life of another,” that the information is “highly offensive to a

                                   2   reasonable person,” and that the information is not of legitimate public concern. Restatement

                                   3   (Second) of Torts § 652D (emphasis added).

                                   4            Thus, Plaintiffs must establish (i) the data is “sensitive,” Popa, 153 F.4th at 790, (ii) the

                                   5   use or disclosure is “highly offensive,” id., (iii) the data is “individually identifiable” to them,

                                   6   Cahen v. Toyota Motor Corp., 717 F. App’x 720, 724 (9th Cir. 2017), and (iv) they maintained a

                                   7   “reasonable expectation of privacy” in the data, see Lloyd v. Facebook, Inc., 2024 WL 3325389, at

                                   8   *2 (9th Cir. July 8, 2024). See Krzyzek, No. 25-cv-05588, 2026 WL 206855, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Jan.

                                   9   27, 2026) (requiring plaintiffs with CIPA, unjust enrichment, and ECPA claims to to “adequately

                                  10   [plead] a ‘highly offensive’ intrusion of privacy that invades a reasonable internet user’s

                                  12   III.     DISCUSSION
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13            Plaintiffs argue that they survive a motion to dismiss based on their core allegation that

                                  14   Capital One used “online tracking technologies” that purportedly disclosed to third parties

                                  15   Plaintiffs’ “Personal and Financial Information” entered when submitting a “credit card

                                  16   application.” Compl. ¶¶ 2–4. Plaintiffs further argue that they have provided evidence that Capital

                                  17   One, through a uniform policy, transmitted their personally identifying and private financial

                                  18   information to third parties in ways its disclosures did not cover, and that both Capital One and the

                                  19   third parties profited as a result. ECF 238 at 3.

                                  20            Defendant argues that Plaintiffs cannot survive a motion to dismiss because Plaintiffs have

                                  21   not demonstrated an injury-in-fact as required by Article III. ECF 219 at 13. Defendant argues

                                  22   that (1) Plaintiffs fail to show that their data were transmitted through most of the challenged

                                  23   technologies, (2) the transmissions that did occur were not “highly offensive” intrusions on

                                  24   privacy, (3) Plaintiffs cannot establish a reasonable expectation of privacy over information that

                                  25   was disclosed after reading Capital One’s Privacy Policy, and (4) Plaintiffs cannot show that they

                                  26   will suffer similar injury in the future, so injunctive or declaratory relief is inappropriate. Id. at

                                  27   13–14.

                                  28

                                                   i.   Plaintiffs Present a Genuine Dispute of Material Fact Regarding Whether
                                   1                    Their Individually Identifiable Data was Transmitted to Google and Adobe
                                   2          Defendant concedes that the evidence shows two technologies transmitted their

                                   3   information before this lawsuit was filed: Adobe Analytics (both Plaintiffs) and Google Ads Data

                                   4   Hub (Ms. Williams). ECF 252 at 5. Defendant instead argues that Plaintiffs have no injury

                                   5   because the transmissions did not include information individually identifiable to the Plaintiffs.

                                   6          The Court agrees that Plaintiffs must show that transmissions to Adobe are “individually

                                   7   identifiable,” Cahen, 717 F. App’x at 724, because “disclosure of non-individually identifiable

                                   8   data is insufficient to give rise to an injury-in-fact.” Mikulsky v. Noom, Inc., 2024 WL 251171, at

                                   9   *4 (S.D. Cal. Jan. 22, 2024). Plaintiffs’ intention to represent a class also does not affect the

                                  10   analysis because they still “must allege and show that they personally have been injured, not that

                                  11   [the] injury has been suffered by other, unidentified members of the class.” Lewis v. Casey, 518

                                  12   U.S. 343, 357 (1996)
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          Defendant acknowledges that under Bowen v. Energizer Holdings, Inc., courts cannot

                                  14   resolve “material factual disputes” at the dismissal stage when “merits issues and jurisdictional

                                  15   issues are intertwined.” 118 F.4th 1134, 1143 (9th Cir. 2024); see also In re Splunk Inc. v. Sec.

                                  16   Litig., 592 F. Supp. 3d 919, 946 (N.D. Cal. 2022) (finding that the Court “may not resolve factual

                                  17   disputes at the pleading stage”).

                                  18          Defendant argues that Adobe was provided with anonymous transmissions including a

                                  19   unique number randomly generated by Adobe which corresponds to a similar randomly generated

                                  20   ID created by Capital One. ECF 220-1 at 16. Adobe, Defendant insists, does not know who the

                                  21   randomly generated ID number belongs to. Id. However, Plaintiffs presented showing that the

                                  22   data transmitted to Google includes personally identifiable information. Plaintiffs argue that this

                                  23   information can be “de-anonymized” such that individuals may be identified. ECF 239-1 at 22.

                                  24   Plaintiff’s expert, Dr. Egelman claims he was able to de-anonymize a list of emails that were

                                  25   supposedly anonymized by Capital One. Id. Plaintiff further argues that Adobe public touts that it

                                  26   can and does use supposedly anonymous data to identify people. Id. at 21. A genuine issue of

                                  27   material fact exists as to whether the “anonymized” data provided to Adobe can be traced back to

                                  28   individual Capital One customers. Plaintiffs’ need to demonstrate that information that personally
                                                                                          8

                                   1   identifies them was transmitted is common to both the merits and the jurisdictional elements their

                                   2   claims. The Court “must leave the resolution of material factual disputes to the trier of fact when

                                   4   Bowen,118 F.4th at 1144.

                                   9   43

                                                        website. A business utilizing this technology can then access useful

                                   6           I.   LEGAL STANDARD
                                   7          Generally, a party seeking to file document under seal for a “discovery motion unrelated to

                                   8   the merits of the case” need only demonstrate “good cause to seal.” Ctr. for Auto Safety v.

                                   9   Chrysler Grp., LLC, 809 F.3d 1092, 1097 (9th Cir. 2016). However, where the “requested relief

                                  10   would . . . restrict the evidence [a party] could present at trial” courts have found that the motion is

                                  11   “more than tangentially related to the merits of [a] case.” Aero v. Boeing Co., 2024 WL 357787, at

                                  12   *2 (W.D. Wash. Jan. 31, 2024); Tan v. Konnektive Rewards, LLC, 2023 WL 2336893, at *3 (S.D.
Northern District of California

                                  13   Cal. Mar. 2, 2023).

                                  14          Courts have recognized a “general right to inspect and copy public records and documents,

                                  15   including judicial records.” Nixon v. Warner Commc’ns, Inc., 435 U.S. 589, 597 & n.7 (1978).

                                  16   “Unless a particular court record is one ‘traditionally kept secret,’ a ‘strong presumption in favor

                                  17   of access’ is the starting point.” Kamakana v. City and Cnty. of Honolulu, 447 F.3d 1172, 1178

                                  18   (9th Cir. 2006) (quoting Foltz v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 331 F.3d 1122, 1135 (9th Cir.

                                  19   2003)). To overcome this strong presumption, a party seeking to seal a judicial record must

                                  20   articulate “compelling reasons supported by specific factual findings that outweigh the general

                                  21   history of access and the public policies favoring disclosure.” Id. at 1178-79 (internal quotation

                                  22   marks and citations omitted). “In general, ‘compelling reasons’ . . . exist when such ‘court files

                                  23   might have become a vehicle for improper purposes,’ such as the use of records to gratify private

                                  24   spite, promote public scandal, circulate libelous statements, or release trade secrets.” Id. at 1179

                                  25   (citing Nixon, 435 U.S. at 598). “The mere fact that the production of records may lead to a

                                  26   litigant’s embarrassment, incrimination, or exposure to further litigation will not, without more,

                                  27   compel the court to seal its records.” Id. (citing Foltz, 331 F.3d at 1136).

                                  28          Finally, request to seal satisfies compelling reasons standard where those requests are
